agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: The spectra are smooth: no matrix has an isolated top singular value out of line with its neighbours. So there is no sign of a planted low-rank defect, and the weakness looks intrinsic to the model's computation. I've closed the MLP repetition-neuron line (zeroing 76 neurons did not loosen loops) and the weight-anomaly line. To find a mechanism worth targeting, I need a sharper picture of the finished wrong answers, which are the majority of failures. I'll print a few problems next to the start of the model's wrong answer, under 300 characters each, and a tally of a simple failure signature. Does the first sentence restate the problem's numbers correctly, or does the model state irrelevant variables? The aim is a recurring, identifiable error pattern, for example misreading quantities at the start, that could connect to a specific circuit. If the errors are heterogeneous, I'll fall back to the style and loop mechanisms, where the evidence is crisper.

These wrong answers fail at the setup, not the arithmetic. The model binds quantities to the wrong things: "15 minutes/turkey" where the problem says per pound, multiplying miles per gallon by "3 cars", forgetting the ×7 for a week, and "needs 3 cups and has 3 cups". These binding errors are heterogeneous and hard to pin to one component. The more tractable lever may be the response mode chosen at the first answer token. The model runs either an instruction-style markdown mode ("Here's how to solve...") or a pretraining-like LaTeX mode ("Let $X$ be..."), and the plain mode is noticeably more accurate when it finishes (37% vs 25%). Style may simply correlate with problem type, though. So I'll stratify by difficulty, using the number of steps in the reference solution as a proxy, and compare the two styles' accuracy within strata. I'll also check how strongly the last-prompt-token state predicts style, to see whether a single decision direction exists. A consistent plain-over-markdown advantage within strata, with an early, clean style decision, would make style steering worth a causal test. No advantage within strata would mean the gap is problem selection, and I'd drop the idea.

Within every difficulty stratum, plain-style answers are more accurate than markdown-style ones: 39 vs 34% at 2 steps, 30 vs 17% at 3, 23 vs 12% at 4, and 12 vs 2% at 5+. The plain advantage averages around 9 points, so it is not just problem selection, though causality still needs a steering test. The style is largely decided before the first answer token: a difference-of-means direction on the last-prompt-token state separates the styles with AUC 0.78 at layer 5, rising to 0.97 by layer 15 and 0.99 by layer 20. That pins the decision to the middle layers. To find the components that make it, I'll look at MLP neurons at the last prompt token. For each neuron I'll compute its activation difference between plain and markdown problems (standardized), and the alignment of its write direction (post_feedforward_layernorm weight times its down_proj column) with the style direction in the residual after that layer. Neurons with a large activation difference and a strongly aligned write, concentrated in a few layers, would be the style switch. Scaling them is a clean, targeted intervention to test at several strengths.

Neuron-level attribution of the style decision is diffuse: no handful of neurons dominates, and scores are small and spread across layers. As with the loop neurons, the decision looks distributed, so a residual-direction intervention fits better than neuron ablation. Gemma's post-attention and post-feedforward RMSNorms mean that a sublayer's write along a residual direction d equals the component of its pre-norm output along d ⊙ (1+w), divided by the RMS. So "remove or reverse direction d in this layer's output" can be built exactly at the pre-norm level by projecting d ⊙ (1+w) out of o_proj or down_proj. First I need to know which layers write the style direction. I'll take the unit style direction at layer 20, where separation is near-perfect. Then, at the last prompt token, I'll measure each layer's residual update along it (overall mean and plain-minus-markdown difference). A few layers with large differential writes would be the targets for a reversal or projection edit, tested causally at several strengths. If the write is spread evenly across all layers, a single-layer edit won't work and I'd need a multi-layer one.
